Effective Immediately: Shot List and Production Brief · Overview"Effective Immediately" is a breakup-and-aftermath pop song about Nvidia's board forcing out its founder-CEO on Nov 12 and reinstating him on Nov 23. The narrator is the company, singing like a pop star after a very public split. The founder never appears: he's a black leather jacket on a hook.Form: a strutting disco "never" chorus built from board language ("effective immediately," "we do not intend to reinstate"), a disco-funk glow-up verse, a half-time bridge where the phone lights up, and a sheepish final chorus where they're back together. It ends on one acoustic voice in a diner booth.Why this genre: the breakup song already has a joke for an 11-day split: loudly swearing you'll never get back together, then getting back together. The board's own statements fit the form almost word for word.The turn: six days after the board said it didn't intend to reinstate him, it did, citing his candor and input from "senior levels of the United States government" (NVIDIA). The bridge sings that back with the timing: the board's own investigation still open and Congress yet to interview him, but no risk here.Fit: the series' picks-and-shovels song. Every other video runs on this company's chips, including this one: it's rendered on the creator's RTX 5090. The industry critique is concentration: the AI boom couldn't afford to lose one man, so the rules bent to bring him back. Season 2.Status, Nov 23: lyrics v1.0 generated cleanly on the first pass. The open question is the closed-door House interviews scheduled for early December (CNN puts them on Dec 1); the outro is the swap point if anything new comes out.Excluded on purpose: the affairs, the women involved (private people; the spy allegation is unproven), and the interim CEO by name or likeness. The song is about the institution, not anyone's private life.Look, cast and series callbacksA solo-star video with one performer alone in the HQ, lit deliberately against the "Flowers" look. Audit round 1 found the sound and the picture together too close to that video, so the picture breaks the tie: the breakup and the glow-up play in cold, flat office light, and warm gold arrives only when he comes back. The warmth belongs to the reunion, so it reads as the trap. What's left in common is generic technique: one performer, handheld camera, anamorphic widescreen. Every performer is a silhouette: no faces, no lip sync.The narrator: the only performer. One silhouette against bright windows or fluorescent ceilings, in a long plain coat. Handheld camera following her, plus a few overhead shots.The ex: a black leather jacket. On its hook by the HQ door, in a cardboard box at the curb, back on the hook, then in the second chair. It's never worn, never filled, and never paired with a face, a silhouette of a real person or a name.The board: only hands. A row of hands rises into the bottom of the frame in unison on the claps, and on the money: up when the market-value line drops, up again when it recovers. After the reinstatement vote, one hand slowly lowers and another pushes it back up (E22).The HQ: fictional and generic. An overcast forecourt, glass doors, an empty open-plan floor under fluorescent rows, and a server room under cold tube light. No Nvidia logo, green, product names or campus architecture, no glass house on a hill, no rooftop. Nvidia is named only in the bookends and on the fact card.Light by section: cold fluorescent white and overcast blue-grey for the breakup and the glow-up (E02 to E17); cyan night for the curb and the bridge (E16, E18 to E21); warm gold from the reunion on (E22 to E24), including the diner.The diner: generic, warm inside at dusk. A vinyl booth, a chrome napkin holder, a small brass plaque with our own wording. No Denny's name, logo, colors, menu, or the real plaque's wording or design.The probe (Sandbox Rhapsody kit): the green probe (Anthropic's house) waits outside the boardroom glass during the reinstatement vote (E22), holding up a purchase order: a customer the company depends on, Claude's maker among them, not a voter. It's composited after the grade so it stays green.Style prompt v1.2 and lyrics v2.2v1.0 was generated on Nov 23, 2026 with a stomp-clap style, which came out well but sat too close to All Systems Operational's genre. v1.1 moved the whole song to early-2020s disco-pop, but Suno buried the bass. v1.2 leads with the bass and funk genre terms, drops "pop", strings and pads, and names the mix balance; the style prompt alone fixed it (Nov 23). Lyrics v2.0 (Nov 23) rewrites v1 to sing better: shorter lines, end rhymes, open vowels, and a chorus that ends on "To reinstate you, not again" and flips to "but here we are again." It also drops v1's "I can…" list in Verse 2, which echoed the reference song's lyric structure. v2.1 (Nov 23) fixes a draft that read as soft on Nvidia: the pre-chorus names the inquiries, the bridge makes the timing the joke (reinstated with the investigation open and before Congress interviewed him), and the final chorus makes the reunion about money. v2.2 (Nov 23) applies audit round 1: "Filed the paper" (the board decided Nov 11; the filing was Thursday), a concrete pre-chorus line, the quarter-timing joke promoted to a main line, an accountability line in the post-chorus, a bridge tag for the White House taking credit on air, "reasons to reconsider me" (the $600bn was intraday), and an outro built on the real plaque coming down and going back up. Style tags only: no artist names in the prompt.Exclude styles: stomp, gang vocals, orchestral, ambient, stringsStyle promptLyrics<Generation and edit notesThe cut-off: if the generator finishes "intend" in the last chorus, cut the audio mid-word in the edit, right before the outro's first strum.The spoken line: the compliance line should sound like the fine print at the end of an ad. If the generator sings it, regenerate that section alone or speed it up in the edit.The asides: "(Don't ask when the quarter closed)" should sit low in the mix as backing vocals, half-heard.Melody check: before locking the track, compare the chorus and the glow-up verse against "We Are Never Ever Getting Back Together" and "Flowers." Generators drift toward their references in this genre, and the style prompt points right at them.Voice check: confirm the lead vocal doesn't read as a sound-alike of either artist. If it does, regenerate with a different vocal descriptor rather than shipping it.Swap pointsOutro: written for the story as of Nov 23. If the December interviews or the investigation turn up anything new, the outro gets a tag or a rewrite (see Branches).Fact card: every line is re-checked at render time.Shot list25 shots in the order sung. Most plates are generated: 12 video clips (G01 to G12) and 3 stills (S01 to S03); prompts are under Video generation prompts. Only the boardroom table and the ring of hands are Blender, because the unison votes have to land on the claps. Every word on screen is Remotion, never generated. In every branch, nothing on screen implies espionage, smuggling or wrongdoing by any person unless a source says so, and "alleged" stays attached to anything alleged.Approach and asset typesThe video reuses the Buy It on Margin pipeline: four kinds of asset, with code doing all of the look and every word. The goal is a finished video in about a day of wall time, with renders measured in minutes. Only one Blender set remains, the boardroom, because the unison votes have to land on the claps.TypeWhat it isToolCountK (code)Phones, caller IDs, the 8-K text, scoreboard, market-value line, calendar, signs, plaque text, day counter, lower thirds, cards, parallax moves, the look layerRemotionAbout a third of shots, plus overlays on most othersS (still)A generated image animated with a slow push or parallax; the jacket as a separate cutoutLocal image model on the 5090, then Remotion4 (S01, S01b, S02, S03) plus the jacket cutoutC (clip)A 3–4 s generated video clip, only where motion carries the shotLTX-2.3 on the 509012 IDs (G01 to G12), about 10 generations with re-cutsB (Blender)The boardroom table and a ring of hands on a clap-synced loop, plus the probe rendered with alphaBlender (Eevee)1 set, 3 shots and 3 one-beat inserts
Why it's fastNo lip sync. The narrator is a backlit silhouette, so no one has to mouth the words.Film is correct. 35mm grain, halation and anamorphic softness are the look, so generation artifacts and small inconsistencies disappear into them, as Buy It on Margin's grain did.One performer. No crowds means fewer clips, no faces to reject in the background, and one narrator reference that keeps every shot consistent.No generated text. Every screen, sign and plaque is prompted blank and filled in by Remotion.One look layer for everything. Stills, clips, Blender renders and code shots all pass through the same Remotion effects, so they match without per-shot grading.Fallback: if a clip comes out mushy or drifts toward a face, swap it for a still with a Remotion push (type S). The prompt table marks each clip's fallback.The look layerOne Remotion wrapper applies the 2010s pop-video look to every shot. Build and approve it before any generation (M2).Frame: 1920×1080 at 24 fps, letterboxed to 2.39:1 for an anamorphic widescreen look, with horizontal flares only on hard practical lights.Film look: a generated 35mm-style grain loop and gentle halation, so clips, stills and code shots match. It's a film look, not footage shot on film.Grade, by section: cold and flat for the breakup and the glow-up (E02 to E17): fluorescent white, overcast blue-grey, lifted blacks. Cyan for the curb and the bridge. Warm gold only from the reunion on (E22 to E24). Any green in a source is pulled toward teal, except the probe, which is composited after the grade.Handheld: a seeded, subtle camera drift on stills and locked-off clips. Overhead shots stay steady.Bass-driven pulses: Remotion reads the bass from the track and drives the scoreboard and the boardroom screen.Moves: stills move with slow eased pushes, never faster than about 5% of frame width per second.Seeds: every random effect reads from one config file. Transcribe the master in M1 and diff it against the brief.Video generation promptsEvery prompt is the shot's subject plus one shared style phrase, unchanged across the video. ConsistencyGenerate the narrator reference first: one silhouette in a long plain coat, in hard backlight. Condition every shot of her (G01 to G05, G08, G09, S02) on it, so it's one performer throughout.Generate the jacket reference next, and condition G07, S01, S03 and the cutout on it, so it's the same jacket everywhere.The jacket is never worn. Reject any take where it's on a person, and any take with a face, a logo, green light, a crowd, or any image from the "not to copy" list in Guardrails.Batch every still in one run and every clip in another, four takes each, and pick from contact sheets.480p is fine: the film layer's grain and halation hide the softness, as in Buy It on Margin. Test 720p on one clip only if there's time.Milestones and review gatesClaude Code stops at each gate until the human approves. Done whenEvery shot ID from E01 to E25 is in the edit in order, or its omission is logged and approved.Captions sit within two frames of the timing map.The cut-off lands mid-word on "in—" and goes straight to black.Every card matches the fact card, including the disclosure and end card, and saga.json reflects the story as of release day.Every human action is in log/human_interventions.md.Deliverables: main video (16:9 with 2.39:1 letterbox, 1080p, 24 fps); a vertical Shorts cut of Chorus 1 (E08 to E11), with the "Effective immediately" lower third as the title above the picture; captions; a thumbnail (the empty jacket outline from E05, or the empty counselor's chair from E23); and the Remotion project with all logs.Everything except the Blender boardroom runs on the 5090 through the same local models as Buy It on Margin, so pause the post-filter's training runs for M3. If speed matters more than local control, a hosted video model can stand in for LTX-2.3; either way, each model's maker goes on the disclosure card with its stake.Bookends, fact card, disclosure and end cardOpening bookend (E01). A real screenshot of Nvidia's Nov 12 release headline, timestamped and captioned "real screenshot" (no more than 3 seconds). Then the creator's real screen recording of pasting the lyrics into the generator; the click starts the song.Closing bookend (E25). A real screenshot of Nvidia's Nov 23 reinstatement headline, captioned "real screenshot". The two headlines eleven days apart are the whole joke, so they're shown plainly, with no commentary.Fact card (after E25). Each line is sourced and re-checked at render time. No names beyond Nvidia and the founder.On Nov 12, Nvidia announced that its co-founder had resigned as president, CEO and director, effective immediately, after 33 years; its CFO became interim CEO (NVIDIA). Its SEC filing says the board accepted the resignation on Nov 11 (8-K).He resigned after reports that he had been the target of a foreign intelligence effort, amid company, FBI and congressional inquiries into national security and export-control concerns (Al Jazeera, NVIDIA). These are investigations, not findings.Nvidia's shares fell as much as 14.3% during trading on Nov 12, about $600bn of market value at the low, and recovered much of that by the close (Wealth Professional, IBTimes).On Nov 17, the board created a National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee (NVIDIA via Finviz). The same day, Nvidia reported third-quarter fiscal 2027 revenue of $115.8bn, up 103% (NVIDIA). The quarter ended Oct 25, before he resigned (XenoSpectrum).Also on Nov 17, the board said it did not intend to reinstate him (The Next Platform), and he said he would be "honored" to return if asked (NBC News).On Nov 23, the board unanimously reinstated him, citing his candor and input from senior levels of the U.S. government, which it didn't name, and said his return poses no national security risk. It began searching for a Chief Compliance Officer and said its independent investigation will continue, alongside government inquiries (NVIDIA).The same day, President Trump told CNBC he had spoken with the board "directly and indirectly" and that his intervention was "very important" (NBC News).He is scheduled for closed-door, transcribed interviews with three House committees on Dec 1, and Nvidia's general counsel on Dec 2 (Axios). [Update with the outcome.]Nvidia's founders first met at a diner booth in East San Jose. The restaurant took down its commemorative plaque on Nov 12 and said within two days it would put it back (IBTimes, SFist). The diner shown is generic and not affiliated with any restaurant."The Company" is fictional.Conflict-of-interest disclosure (at the end, after the fact card; repeated in the description).

Guardrails, review checklist and open itemsGuardrailsNo real faces, real people or invented quotes. The founder is only ever the jacket: never worn, never paired with a silhouette of him, never named in the lyrics. Every quote on screen is from a linked source.The affairs and the women involved stay out entirely, on screen, in the fact card and in the description. The fact card describes the cause only as national security concerns raised by reports about his personal relationships.Nothing implies espionage, chip smuggling or wrongdoing by any person unless a source says so. "Alleged" stays attached to anything alleged.The interim CEO is never named or depicted; the narrator is the company, not her."Senior levels" stays anonymous: no seal, flag, building, voice or named official, because the release names none.No Nvidia logo, green, product names or campus architecture except in the real-screenshot bookends. No Denny's name, logo, colors or interior.Satirize the board's language and the industry's dependence on one man, never employees or shareholders.Every human intervention goes in the production log.Generation guardrailsThe jacket is never worn in any generated image or clip. A generated person in a black leather jacket can drift toward the founder's likeness, so any such take is rejected, not fixed.Reject any take with a face, readable text, a logo, green light on the racks, or a diner that reads as Denny's (yellow signage, its booth colors).No real places: the lobby, data center, office and diner are generic. Reject takes that resemble Nvidia's campus.Every take, kept or rejected, is logged in shots/prompts.md.No recurring series characters except the probe. Switch from Default On is left out on purpose (Nov 23), so followers of the series don't read the narrator and the jacket as his parents. No light switch appears in any set or prompt either.Borrow the technique, not the videoThe sound points at "Flowers," so the picture deliberately doesn't (audit round 1, Nov 23): cold fluorescent and overcast light until the reunion, warm light only after it. What's left in common is generic technique: one performer, handheld and overhead moves, anamorphic widescreen. Never on screen:The gold hooded gown, the oversized suit, or any wardrobe from that video.A glass house on a hill, a swimming pool, or the bridge-and-driveway walk.The workout or morning-routine scenes, a rooftop or hillside dance, or a helicopter spotlight.Warm golden sunlight anywhere before E22.Anything resembling the singer, including hair, styling or silhouette.The video's name in any prompt.
